title: Political Economy, Political Sociology and the Limits of Comparison

cards.h: Money, society and the limits of comparison
cards.b:
This lesson covers three linked ideas. Political economy asks how politics and the economy shape each other. Political sociology asks how social groups, classes, cleavages and culture shape politics. And the limits of comparison asks the honest question: how far can we trust cross-country comparisons?

Together they move you from "what do institutions look like?" (the previous lesson) to "why do they look that way, and what are the limits to what we know?"

For the exam, learn a handful of anchor works with years: Polanyi (1944), Esping-Andersen (1990), Hall and Soskice (2001), Lipset and Rokkan (1967), Putnam (1993), Sartori (1970). Add India: Bardhan, Rudolph and Rudolph, Varshney.

A top answer ends with the limits: small number of cases, selection bias, concept stretching, and Eurocentrism.

Political economy studies how states and markets interact: who gets what, when and how, and who decides.

There are several traditions.

  • Classical liberal. Adam Smith (The Wealth of Nations, 1776) and David Ricardo. Free markets create wealth. The state should be limited.
  • Marxist. Karl Marx (Capital, 1867): the economic base shapes politics. The state serves the dominant class.
  • Statist and nationalist. Friedrich List, The National System of Political Economy (1841): protect infant industries.
  • Keynesian. John Maynard Keynes (The General Theory, 1936): governments should manage demand.
  • Institutionalist. Institutions shape economic results (Douglass North).
  • Public choice. Politicians and bureaucrats follow self-interest (James Buchanan, Gordon Tullock). Anne Krueger (1974) coined rent-seeking.

Karl Polanyi, The Great Transformation (1944): markets are not natural. They are created by states. Unregulated markets trigger a "double movement" as society pushes back to protect itself. Markets must stay embedded in society.

cards.h: Varieties of capitalism and welfare regimes
cards.b:
Varieties of Capitalism

Peter Hall and David Soskice (eds.), Varieties of Capitalism (2001). Firms solve coordination problems differently. In liberal market economies (US, UK) markets and competition do the work. In coordinated market economies (Germany, Japan, Nordic) institutions like unions, banks and employer groups coordinate. Each has comparative advantage: radical innovation versus incremental, high-quality production.

Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism

Gosta Esping-Andersen (1990). Decommodification is the degree to which people can live without selling their labour. He found three regimes: liberal (US: means-tested aid), conservative-corporatist (Germany, France: social insurance linked to jobs) and social-democratic (Sweden, Denmark: universal benefits).

Critiques: they ignore the Global South, the family and gender (feminists such as Ann Orloff and Jane Lewis), and the role of finance.

• Gerschenkron, Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962): late developers need the state and banks to push industry.
  • Developmental state. Chalmers Johnson, MITI and the Japanese Miracle (1982); Alice Amsden on South Korea (Asia's Next Giant, 1989); Robert Wade on Taiwan (Governing the Market, 1990). A competent bureaucracy guides firms, protects them for a while, and demands export performance.
  • Embedded autonomy. Peter Evans, Embedded Autonomy (1995): the state needs ties to business, but also independence from it. Compare predatory states (Zaire under Mobutu).
  • Corporatism. Philippe Schmitter, "Still the Century of Corporatism?" (1974): peak organisations of labour and business bargain with the state, as in Austria and Sweden. This contrasts with pluralism.
  • Institutions and growth. Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson, Why Nations Fail (2012): inclusive institutions create prosperity; extractive ones do not. They won the 2024 Nobel in economics, with Simon Johnson.

Seymour Martin Lipset and Stein Rokkan, in Party Systems and Voter Alignments (1967), argued that Western European party systems "froze" around four cleavages produced by two revolutions: the National Revolution (centre-periphery, state-church) and the Industrial Revolution (land-industry, owner-worker).

Lipset's earlier Political Man (1960) linked democracy to economic development and social conditions.

Ronald Inglehart's postmaterialism (The Silent Revolution, 1977) added a new value cleavage: security versus self-expression.

cards.h: Civil society, social capital and elites
cards.b:
• Social capital. Robert Putnam, Making Democracy Work (1993), compared regional governments in Italy. Northern regions, with dense civic associations and trust, did better than the south. Bowling Alone (2000) argued that civic life in the US was declining.
  • Civil society. Tocqueville praised associations. Gramsci saw civil society as the arena of hegemony. Post-1989 scholars saw it as a force against authoritarianism.
  • Elite theory. Gaetano Mosca and Vilfredo Pareto: every society is ruled by an organised minority. Robert Michels's "iron law of oligarchy" (Political Parties, 1911) argued that even democratic parties become oligarchic. C. Wright Mills, The Power Elite (1956), described a military-industrial-political elite. Robert Dahl's Who Governs? (1961) replied with pluralism.
  • Participation and mobilisation. Voting, protest and social movements (Charles Tilly; resource mobilisation theory).
  • Class and identity. Ethnicity, religion, gender, caste and region as bases of politics.

Comparison is powerful, but it has well-known limits.

  • Many variables, few cases. Lijphart's "small N" problem. Dozens of factors, only a handful of countries.
  • Concept stretching. Giovanni Sartori, "Concept Misformation in Comparative Politics" (1970): a concept like "party" or "democracy" gets stretched to fit different contexts until it loses meaning. His "ladder of abstraction" shows that broader concepts cover more cases but say less.
  • Selection bias. Choosing cases because they had a certain outcome (revolutions only) distorts causal claims.
  • Galton's problem. Cases are not independent. Ideas and institutions spread by diffusion and colonialism.
  • Context and equivalence. The same institution (a parliament, a vote) works differently in different settings. Data may not be comparable.
  • Ethnocentrism. Concepts drawn from Western experience may not suit the Global South.
  • Values. Choice of topic and standard reflects the researcher's views.
  • Prediction. Social systems are open: people learn and change.

Scientific route

Gary King, Robert Keohane and Sidney Verba, Designing Social Inquiry (1994): qualitative research should follow the logic of statistical inference. Increase the number of observations and be careful about selection.

Qualitative route

Henry Brady and David Collier, Rethinking Social Inquiry (2004), and Charles Ragin's The Comparative Method (1987) with Qualitative Comparative Analysis: case knowledge and process tracing give causal insight even with few cases.

Mixed methods and area studies

Combine large-N data with deep case studies. Use "nested analysis". Respect area expertise.

Post-colonial and critical

Question whose categories count. Partha Chatterjee, Mahmood Mamdani and Edward Said ask us to read non-Western politics on its own terms.

The answer for the exam: comparison remains valuable, but use cautious claims, clear concepts and multiple methods.

cards.h: Political economy and society in India
cards.b:
• Pranab Bardhan, The Political Economy of Development in India (1984): the state is shaped by three dominant proprietary classes: industrial capitalists, rich farmers and the professionals and bureaucrats. Their rivalry slowed public investment and growth.
  • Rudolph and Rudolph, In Pursuit of Lakshmi (1987): India's political economy has a "command polity" of the state and a "demand polity" of groups.
  • Atul Kohli, Democracy and Discontent (1990): the crisis of governability. State-Directed Development (2004) compared India, South Korea, Brazil and Nigeria.
  • Reforms. The 1991 liberalisation shifted India from state-led to market-led growth, while keeping a strong welfare agenda (MGNREGA, 2005; food security law, 2013).
  • Society. Ashutosh Varshney, Ethnic Conflict and Civic Life (2002), applied Putnam's logic to Hindu-Muslim riots. Towns with inter-communal civic associations saw less violence than towns without them.
  • Cleavages. Caste, religion, language and region define India's party system, unlike Europe's class cleavages (Chandra, Yadav).

Comparative limits are clear in India: concepts like "class" or "civil society" need adjustment (Chatterjee's "political society").

"What are the limitations of the comparative method in political analysis?"
"Discuss the political economy approach to the study of comparative politics."
"How do social cleavages shape party systems? Illustrate."
"Compare the developmental state with the neoliberal state."

Structure: start with a definition. For political economy: traditions (liberal, Marxist, Polanyi), then Varieties of Capitalism and Esping-Andersen in boxes, and the developmental state. For political sociology: Lipset and Rokkan's cleavages, Putnam, elite theory. For limits: small N, concept stretching (Sartori), selection bias, Galton's problem, ethnocentrism, and the responses (mixed methods). Close with India: Bardhan, Varshney, Chatterjee.

Show you can criticise the tools you learn.

o: Markets are created by states and need to be embedded in society
quiz.w: His 'double movement': society protects itself from unregulated markets.
